price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

methodological_questions: Is the recommended mix derived independently of the outcome it is meant to predict (leakage, outcome-derived labels)?
Does adherence predict winning after controlling for team quality and opponent?
Does adherence beat a placebo or baseline such as the team's modal play type or a random mix?
How are score-state reverse causation and multiple testing handled?

historical_evidence.finding: The engine's top recommended play type was compared with the team's modal play type in playoff series. The calibrated headline hit rate was 69.8% (37/53). Comparisons against a banned-PT DRIVE-modal were 85.7% (12/14) and clean comparisons were 64.1% (25/39). The uncalibrated archival rate was 51.7% (31/60). Recorded failure mechanism: C_artifact. Limits: small sample. Risks: leakage/lookahead and sample size. No bootstrap CI was computed.

Ranked playsheet validation on 10 series. The full-rank Spearman was null (rho=-0.0639, p=0.0997, n=665). The pairwise comparison BEST 1.257 PPP (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 PPP (n=160) gave Mann-Whitney p=0.004. Limits recorded: leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample. Risks recorded include drift/nonstationarity.

The Possession Control Index gain over ORtg was driven by a leakage component that tracks DRtg (corr +0.894). The offensive-control increment was dR2=+0.005. The baseline omitted defense by construction (Net=ORtg-DRtg). Risks recorded: leakage/lookahead and mechanical floor.

A proxy matchup-conditioned play-type picker showed a possession-level gain (C gamma +0.0714 PPP, n=16,921 cells), but proxy agreement with the production engine was only 16.5% (13/79). Recorded problems: in-sample contamination of regular-season aggregates, iid standard errors, and coverage of only 35.7% clear recommendations.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level hit rate of the engine's recommendation versus the team's modal play type
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as an artifact from a construction, selection or labelling flaw. Limits were small sample (n=53) and leakage/lookahead, with no CI.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked BEST>SECOND>AVOID playsheet validation on 10 series
failed_approaches.why: The full-rank signal was null. The record cites leakage, low measurement reliability and small sample as limits, and the mechanism is recorded as unclear.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Outcome-linked composite index evaluated against Net Rating
failed_approaches.why: Leakage tracked DRtg and the baseline omitted defense by construction. This is the recorded mechanical-floor/leakage artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Proxy engine evaluated on all regular-season games
failed_approaches.why: Proxy fidelity was 16.5%, regular-season aggregates were contaminated in-sample, and the standard errors were iid.

evidence_establishes: Earlier work on closely related recommendation-quality questions found no clean positive result. Two of the four retrieved records are recorded as artifact and two as inconclusive.
Apparent positive signals (69.8% hit rate, pairwise BEST>AVOID, +0.07 PPP) coincided with recorded leakage, small-sample, or proxy-fidelity limits.
Series-level validation with about 53 scoreable units has been tried and was recorded as limited by small sample and leakage.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence to a recommended mix, measured as actual play-type shares, predicts winning. The retrieved records test recommendation hit rates or PPP, not adherence-to-win.
Whether a leakage-free, pre-registered version of the recommendation has any predictive value.
Any effect size for adherence on win probability net of team strength.
own_inferences: The question as posed is ambiguous. 'Adherence' and 'predicts winning' are undefined, and the recommendation is likely derived from the same series it would be tested on, which is outcome-derived by construction.

Adherence probably correlates with winning through team quality, score state (leading teams run different play types) and the opponent's suppression itself, so an unconditioned association would likely be an artifact.
54 series cannot detect modest effects. A game-level analysis with series clustering gives more observations but only modest effective power.
The base expectation, given the history, is that a naive test shows a positive association that shrinks or vanishes after leakage and team-strength controls.
uncertainties: The 54 series are not decomposed by season. It is unclear whether they include partial 2025-26 playoffs, which complete only on 2026-06-21, after the question date.
The exact definition of the 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' and how it is generated are not given in the task.
Records are truncated ('cut'), so details of the retrieved studies were not read in full.
Whether the engine's recommendations can be reconstructed using only pre-series information is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history one might proceed with a straightforward adherence-vs-win regression. The records show repeated leakage and artifact outcomes in this area, so the decision moves to proceed_with_changes with strict ex-ante recommendation freezing, team-strength controls, placebo mixes and a locked confirmatory holdout, and lower expected support.

methodological_questions: Does adherence to a recommended play-type mix predict winning?
How is the recommended mix derived and is it independent of the outcome (leakage, outcome-derived labels)?
Is 54 series enough power for a series-level test?
How to handle regression to the mean, confounding by team quality and opponent, and multiple testing?
Is there a placebo or baseline comparison for adherence?
args.query: Adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended play-type mix (best/avoid) predicting winning at game or series level; prior findings, failed approaches, power, leakage and confounding by team strength

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm wrapping up here, possibly without calling more tools. The question is whether adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning, across 54 series. Several earlier candidates look weak: a leakage artifact on a small sample, one inconclusive result, and another artifact where leakage affected the DRtg tracking. I'm also weighing an inconclusive SF37 result where proxy fidelity sits around 16.5.

I'm working out the sample size: 54 series likely breaks down to about 45 from the three completed playoffs, with some partial 2025-26 series on top, though I'm not certain of that count. I'd propose a pre-registered recommendation fixed before each series, game-level outcomes with team-strength controls, placebo recommendations as falsification checks, and the completed 2025-26 playoffs as a holdout, then estimate what effect size that design could detect.

I'm also checking the power figure: with 54 series, a correlation around 0.38 would be detectable, which seems reasonable. The mechanical risks are a separate concern: trailing teams change their play types in garbage time, so adherence can track the score rather than the recommendation, and measuring adherence on possessions whose points are already fixed, or tying the recommendation to suppression observed within the same series, would leak the outcome into the predictor.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm wrapping up here, possibly without calling more tools. The question is whether adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning, across 54 series. Several earlier candidates look weak: a leakage artifact on a small sample, one inconclusive result, and another artifact where leakage affected the DRtg tracking. I'm also weighing an inconclusive SF37 result where proxy fidelity sits around 16.5.

I'm working out the sample size: 54 series likely breaks down to about 45 from the three completed playoffs, with some partial 2025-26 series on top, though I'm not certain of that count. I'd propose a pre-registered recommendation fixed before each series, game-level outcomes with team-strength controls, placebo recommendations as falsification checks, and the completed 2025-26 playoffs as a holdout, then estimate what effect size that design could detect.

I'm also checking the power figure: with 54 series, a correlation around 0.38 would be detectable, which seems reasonable. The mechanical risks are a separate concern: trailing teams change their play types in garbage time, so adherence can track the score rather than the recommendation, and measuring adherence on possessions whose points are already fixed, or tying the recommendation to suppression observed within the same series, would leak the outcome into the predictor.
